strengths: Originality/significance: Treating GHN-generated weight matrices as spatial fields and patchifying them for diffusion is an interesting synthesis of hypernetworks, flexible-resolution transformers, and weight generation. Joint architecture-and-weight generation is also a potentially useful direction.

Soundness: The generated policies are evaluated by execution in three ManiSkill3 tasks rather than only by parameter-space proxies. Table 2 shows a substantial advantage over D2NWG on held-out architecture combinations, especially for PickCube and StackCubeEasy.

The comparison between 35 GHN- and SGD-generated policies, together with the larger appendix analysis, provides suggestive evidence that the CNN-based GHN induces repeatable spatial patterns without obvious loss of policy performance.
Presentation: The paper is generally well organized, and the framework diagrams, result tables, appendices, and rollout visualizations make the proposed pipeline easy to follow.

Limitations and ethics: The paper discloses its restriction to small, fixed-depth MLP policies and simulation. No immediate material ethical issue is apparent, although the impact discussion is cursory.
weaknesses: The central width-agnostic claim is not demonstrated. Every tested layer width comes from the training vocabulary {16,32,64}; the eight held-out cases are only unseen combinations of already-seen widths. Moreover, all experiments use four-hidden-layer MLPs. Thus the results establish interpolation to held-out topology combinations, not zero-shot transfer to unseen widths or depths as repeatedly claimed.

The representation is not intrinsically width-agnostic: every parameter block is padded to a fixed maximum H×W grid determined by M. The paper neither evaluates widths beyond the training range nor explains behavior beyond this preset maximum. The analogy to flexible-resolution image generation therefore does not by itself support the headline conclusion.

The claimed resolution of permutation symmetry is supported mainly by visual banding of weight magnitudes. L2 distance and cosine similarity measure diversity, not alignment or semantic correspondence between coordinates. There is no quantitative alignment statistic, neuron-matching analysis, or controlled comparison against permuted, canonically aligned, or SGD-trained weights.

Key causal ablations are absent. In particular, the paper does not compare CNN and non-CNN GHN decoders, patch and vector tokenization under the same backbone, locally shuffled patches, or NNiT trained on SGD/canonically aligned weights. Consequently, the results cannot establish that GHN-induced locality or patchification specifically causes the reported generalization.

The baseline comparison is insufficiently documented and potentially unfavorable. SANE nearly completely fails even on seen architectures, suggesting that its adaptation or tuning may be unsuitable. D2NWG is described both as architecture-conditioned and as lacking architectural awareness. Exact adaptations, model capacities, tuning budgets, padding conventions, and test-topology handling are not supplied.

Evaluation reports only the top 10 of 100 generated policies, but does not clearly specify the independent selection signal, separate selection and test episodes, or performance of an average/random sample. This best-of-100 protocol can conceal a low success probability and makes the practical generation quality difficult to assess. Results also lack variation across training seeds and statistical tests.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The manuscript omits essential quantities including patch size p, maximum width M, transformer depth/width/head count, positional encoding and padding masks, sampling algorithm and steps, architecture-token decoding, normalization constant and inverse transformation, baseline hyperparameters, exact train/test topology lists, and compute cost. No code or artifact availability statement is provided.

The discrete architecture diffusion mechanism is underspecified: Gaussian noise is applied to learned token embeddings, but the manuscript does not explain how continuous samples are mapped back to valid vocabulary elements or how the stated discretized Gaussian likelihood is implemented. This leaves both the objective and joint-generation procedure difficult to verify.

Several conclusions exceed the evidence, including claims of synthesizing “optimal” weights, resolving permutation ambiguity, generalizing to unseen widths, extending naturally to depth, and potentially generating billion-parameter models. The experiments cover only small MLPs on three closely related simulated tasks, one of which is a simplified custom variant.

strengths: The manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/b7b1f32e40e0436aa457b3f834247aa1/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} explores a potentially useful problem: synthesizing functional weights across multiple MLP architectures rather than training a separate generator for every shape.

Originality: combining patchified weight tensors, architecture tokens, a diffusion transformer, and GHN-generated training data is an interesting synthesis of existing ideas. Joint architecture-and-weight generation is also a promising direction.

Presentation: the paper is generally well organized, and the direct policy-rollout evaluation is more meaningful than evaluating only weight-space reconstruction metrics. The reported NNiT policies achieve strong results on all three simulated tasks, including held-out architecture configurations.

The authors provide useful dataset-generation and optimization details in the appendix, compare against two relevant weight-generation methods, and explicitly acknowledge the current restriction to small MLPs.
weaknesses: Soundness—headline claim mismatch: the experiments do not demonstrate generalization to unseen widths. Training and test architectures both draw widths from the same vocabulary {16, 32, 64}; only combinations of familiar width tokens are held out. Moreover, the method generates a fixed maximal padded grid and crops it, rather than generating additional patches when width increases as claimed. Calling this evidence of “width-agnostic” synthesis or unseen-width transfer is therefore misleading.

Soundness—insufficient causal evidence: no ablation isolates patch tokenization, GHN alignment, the CNN decoder, padding/cropping, or joint training. In particular, there is no NNiT trained on SGD weights, GHN with a non-convolutional decoder, vector-tokenized NNiT, or canonicalized-weight comparison. Consequently, the experiments cannot support the attribution of generalization specifically to patchification or CNN-induced alignment.

The claim that GHNs “resolve permutation ambiguity” is supported mainly by magnitude heatmaps. Visible banding and local correlation do not establish semantic neuron alignment across networks. Nearest-neighbor L2 distance and cosine similarity measure raw parameter diversity, not alignment or absence of functional mode collapse, and are themselves sensitive to scale and permutation. Quantitative spatial-correlation, neuron-matching, permutation-recovery, or re-basin analyses are missing.

The evaluation reports the top 10 of 100 generated policies after rollout-based selection. The selection criterion, whether selection and reporting use independent episodes, and the cost of this validation are unclear. If the same task rollouts select and score policies, the numbers are optimistically biased and no longer show reliable zero-shot deployment. Results for an unconditional sample, all 100 samples, pass@k, and multiple independent model-training seeds are needed.

Baseline evidence is not convincing. SANE obtains nearly zero success even on seen architectures, suggesting that its adaptation or tuning may be unsuitable. The adaptations, model capacities, training budgets, architecture-conditioning mechanisms, and hyperparameters are not documented sufficiently to establish a fair comparison. NNiT is also presented alone for joint generation.

Reproducibility is inadequate. Essential details are absent, including patch size, maximum grid size, transformer depth/width/head count, positional or coordinate encoding, padding masks and padded-region loss treatment, inference sampler and number of denoising steps, discrete-token decoding from diffused continuous embeddings, complete architecture splits, evaluation seeds, and code availability. The description of Gaussian diffusion over embedded discrete architecture tokens is especially incomplete.

Significance is presently limited: evaluation covers only small four-hidden-layer MLPs, three closely related simulated manipulation tasks, a tiny width vocabulary, and a dataset distilled from one teacher through GHNs. There is no evidence for new width values, new depths, larger models, different activation families, other tasks, or architectures outside MLPs. Claims about general-purpose or billion-parameter generation are speculative.

Presentation and limitations: the writing repeatedly turns observations into conclusions—for example, calling Table 2 a “definitive test” and claiming the model has learned the “structural logic of neural design.” The limitations section further asserts that the tested scale “is not a limitation” without evidence. The impact statement is perfunctory and overlooks deployment risks of generated embodied-control policies, although the current simulated experiments pose limited immediate ethical risk. Overall, the central claims substantially exceed the evidence, and the missing ablations and reproducibility details prevent acceptance in the current form.

strengths: Originality/significance: Combining GHN-induced parameter structure, patchified weight representations, and joint architecture-weight diffusion is a novel and potentially useful direction for neural-network synthesis.

Soundness: Directly executing generated policies is a demanding functional evaluation. On eight held-out topology combinations, NNiT substantially outperforms D2NWG on PickCube and StackCubeEasy while maintaining 86–100% top-10 success across the three tasks.
The paper includes useful comparisons with SANE and D2NWG, evaluates both conditional and joint generation, and provides diversity analyses intended to rule out simple parameter-space mode collapse.
Presentation: The motivation, method, deployment pipeline, and main results are generally easy to follow, with polished figures and a reasonably extensive appendix.
The authors honestly acknowledge that experiments are restricted to small, four-hidden-layer MLPs; this is an important limitation and should not itself be penalized.
weaknesses: Soundness: The central “width-agnostic” claim is not established. Training and test architectures use the same width vocabulary {16, 32, 64}; only combinations of already-seen widths are held out. No experiment evaluates a genuinely unseen width value, a width beyond the training range, or a different depth. Moreover, the method generates a fixed maximal H×W grid and crops it, so it remains bounded by a predetermined maximum M. The evidence therefore supports combinatorial interpolation among fixed-size choices, not width-agnostic synthesis.

The claimed resolution of permutation ambiguity is supported mainly by qualitative banding plots. L2 distance and cosine similarity assess diversity, not neuron correspondence or permutation alignment. The paper lacks direct alignment metrics and decisive ablations such as CNN versus non-CNN GHN decoders, randomly permuted or SGD-derived training weights, and patch tokenization versus vectorization under matched capacity.

Evaluation is vulnerable to selection bias: results report the top 10 of 100 generated policies after rollout evaluation, but it is unclear whether separate validation and test episodes are used for selection and reporting. Mean performance over all samples, the fraction of functional generations, uncertainty across generator-training seeds, and results over multiple held-out architecture splits are absent.

The baseline evidence is not fully convincing. SANE fails almost completely even on seen architectures, suggesting that the adaptation or tuning may be unsuitable. Baseline adaptation details, matched parameter counts and compute, and ablations isolating representation from model capacity are not provided. The text also inconsistently describes D2NWG as explicitly architecture-conditioned and as lacking architectural awareness.

The joint-generation claim is weakly evaluated: Table 3 reports policy performance but not the distribution, novelty, or validity of sampled architectures, while Table 4 presents selected examples. Thus the assertion that the model learned broad architecture-weight co-design rather than favoring a small set of templates is not demonstrated.

Reproducibility is inadequate for the main-track standard. Essential specifications—including NNiT depth, hidden dimension, attention configuration, patch size, maximum grid size, parameter count, sampling procedure, architecture-token decoding, baseline configurations, random seeds, compute, and complete PPO/GHN training details—are missing, and no code or data availability statement is given.

Presentation and limitations: Several conclusions substantially exceed the evidence, including claims of “optimal” weights, extension to depth, and feasibility for billion-parameter foundation models. The limitations section dismisses the demonstrated scale restriction as “not a limitation” and omits the fixed maximum width, GHN/data-generation expense, top-10 selection cost, and simulation-only evaluation.

Ethics: There are no human-subject concerns, but the impact statement is boilerplate and does not discuss safety or misuse considerations associated with automatically synthesizing executable robotic policies. This is not independently disqualifying, but it is incomplete.

strengths: Originality/significance: The paper identifies a worthwhile problem—generating functional parameters across multiple MLP architectures—and presents an interesting combination of GHN-induced weight structure, patch tokenization, diffusion transformers, and joint architecture/weight modeling.

Soundness: Direct policy rollouts are a meaningful evaluation of generated weights. NNiT substantially outperforms the adapted D2NWG and SANE baselines on the eight held-out architecture configurations, and Appendix F usefully reports all 80 generated policies in addition to the favorable top-10 metric.

Soundness: The random-permutation ablation is informative: preserving network functions and marginal weight statistics while scrambling coordinates reduces PickCube performance from 78.8% to 0%, providing evidence that consistent coordinate structure matters.

Presentation: The manuscript is generally readable and visually polished. The framework, conditional versus joint generation modes, dataset construction, and deployment procedure are explained coherently.
The authors evaluate three robotic tasks and add an MNIST experiment, weight- and representation-diversity analyses, and joint-sampling statistics rather than relying solely on reconstruction error.
weaknesses: Soundness: The central “width-agnostic” and zero-shot-width claims are not established. Every hidden width comes from the same training vocabulary {16, 32, 64}; the eight test cases are merely unseen combinations of already-seen widths, all with the same four-hidden-layer depth. Moreover, parameters are padded to a fixed maximum grid M, so the method remains bounded by a predetermined maximum width. There is no evaluation on a genuinely unseen width, a width beyond the training range, or a new depth.

Soundness/significance: The training corpus is generated by an ensemble of 128 GHNs, yet the paper omits the decisive direct-GHN baseline on held-out architectures. GHNs are specifically designed to predict parameters for unseen architectures, and the manuscript attributes the useful structure to them. Without comparing NNiT against simply retaining or sampling the GHN ensemble, it is unclear whether the diffusion model adds performance, diversity, efficiency, or practical value over its expensive teacher/data generator.

The proposed explanation of structural alignment is weakly supported. Visual banding, nearest-neighbor distances, cosine similarity, and CKA diversity do not demonstrate neuron-wise correspondence or resolution of permutation symmetry. The reported cross-seed magnitude correlation lacks a precise definition and uncertainty, while the permutation ablation only shows that NNiT relies on consistent coordinates, not that the claimed GHN mechanism uniquely or generally supplies a canonical alignment.

Evaluation is too narrow and statistically incomplete for the central generalization claim. Results appear to come from one trained generator per task, with no training-seed variance or confidence intervals. The selection of the eight held-out configurations is not justified. MNIST reports only one aggregate accuracy without baselines, per-architecture results, or comparison to direct training/GHN generation.

The headline results rely on selecting the top 10 of 100 samples using offline validation. The full-distribution means are only 78.8%, 74.7%, and 54.9% on the three unseen-configuration sets, contradicting the broad abstract-level impression of greater than 85% performance unless the selection protocol is explicitly qualified. Joint-generation results likewise emphasize the selected top 10; before selection only architecture diversity and a 97% “functional” rate are given, without defining functionality or reporting mean task success.

Baseline fairness cannot be assessed. The adaptations of D2NWG and SANE are not specified sufficiently, and SANE's near-total failure even on seen architectures suggests incompatibility or inadequate adaptation rather than a strong comparative test. Missing ablations include a simpler patch-based non-diffusion model, CNN versus non-CNN GHN decoders, patch size, padding/masking and positional encoding choices, conditional-only versus MoNL training, and matched model-capacity comparisons.

Reproducibility is inadequate. Essential details are absent, including patch size p, maximum grid size M, transformer depth/width/heads and parameter count, positional encodings and padding masks, architecture-token decoding, diffusion sampling algorithm and number of steps, normalization reversal, baseline configurations, observation/action specifications, compute requirements, and implementation or data-release information. The custom StackCubeEasy environment is also not specified sufficiently to reconstruct it.

Presentation contains material overclaims: it calls unseen combinations “unseen widths,” states that depth extension follows naturally despite testing only one depth, describes the generated weights as a continuous field without establishing continuity, and speculates about billion-parameter synthesis without relevant evidence. The limitations section explicitly dismisses the tested width/depth restriction as “not a limitation” instead of acknowledging that scalability and extrapolation remain unverified.

Research ethics are not a major immediate concern in this simulation-only study, but the impact statement is boilerplate. A method intended to generate embodied-control policies warrants discussion of validation and safety risks before deployment, failure detection, inherited biases or vulnerabilities from the expert/GHN corpus, and potential malicious or unsafe weight generation.

strengths: Originality/significance: Combining GHN-induced parameter structure, patchwise weight tokenization, and multimodal diffusion is an interesting approach to generating architecture-weight pairs. Directly evaluating generated weights as executable policies is more meaningful than relying only on reconstruction metrics.

Soundness: The reported task performance is promising within the tested setting. NNiT substantially outperforms the adapted D2NWG and SANE baselines on the eight held-out width combinations, and the appendix reports all 80 generated policies in addition to the favorable top-10 metric.

Analysis: The random-permutation ablation is useful evidence that consistent parameter coordinates matter: permuting the GHN corpus preserves policy functions and marginal weight statistics but reduces PickCube success from 78.8% to 0%. The authors also examine weight-space diversity, CKA, and unconditional architecture diversity.

Presentation: The manuscript is generally readable, and its main motivation, representation, and deployment pipeline are communicated clearly through figures and tables. weaknesses: Soundness: The central “width-agnostic” claim is not established. Every experiment uses a fixed four-hidden-layer family and the same three width values {16,32,64}; the eight test architectures are merely unseen combinations of width values repeatedly observed during training. There is no evaluation on a new numerical width, a width beyond the training maximum, or a different depth. Moreover, tensors are padded to a fixed maximum grid M, so the implemented method remains bounded by a predetermined width.

Soundness/significance: The paper omits the most important baseline: direct inference from the GHN that generated the training corpus. The GHN already accepts architectures and produces high-performing weights, including for an architectural search space. Without comparing quality, runtime, diversity, or generalization against the GHN/ensemble itself, it is unclear what practical capability the expensive diffusion model adds beyond distilling and resampling its data source.

Soundness: Evidence for “resolving permutation ambiguity” and inducing meaningful geometry is inadequate. Absolute-weight heatmaps and coordinate correlations show decoder-specific banding, not that corresponding neurons have consistent functional roles. The permutation experiment establishes dependence on a fixed ordering, but it does not show that local patches are the relevant mechanism. No CNN-decoder-versus-nonlocal-decoder ablation, patch-versus-vector ablation under matched modeling capacity, patch-size study, or locality measurement is provided.

Evaluation: Baseline fairness is difficult to assess because the adaptations of SANE and D2NWG are barely specified. SANE achieves only 0–6% success even on seen architectures, suggesting either a severe domain mismatch or an unsuccessful adaptation. The text is also internally inconsistent in describing D2NWG as using “explicit architecture conditioning” and shortly afterward as “lacking explicit architectural awareness.” Comparisons to additional natural alternatives, including an architecture-conditioned patch model without diffusion, are absent.

Evaluation: The headline Table 2 reports the top 10 of 100 generated candidates after environment evaluation. This requires 5,000 rollout episodes per architecture and amounts to strong test-time selection. Although Appendix Table 9 usefully reports the full distribution, mean success falls to 78.8%, 74.7%, and 54.9%, contradicting the abstract and main-text claim of greater than 85% success on unseen topologies. Results also lack variation over independently trained NNiT models, statistical tests, and a precise explanation of what the reported ± values aggregate.

Reproducibility: Essential implementation details are missing: transformer depth/width/head count, patch size p, maximum grid size M, positional encoding, padding/loss masks, architecture-token decoding, sampler and number of sampling steps, normalization constants, parameter count, compute cost, training seeds, and complete baseline modifications. No code or data availability statement is given. The appendix’s optimizer table is insufficient to reproduce the method.

Presentation/technical precision: Several claims overreach the evidence. The paper claims natural depth generalization and potential synthesis of billion-parameter foundation models despite testing only small, fixed-depth MLPs. It calls architecture tokens a “causal prompt” without specifying causal attention, and the dimensional conventions for parameter blocks, the S versus S−1 layer count, and the choice W=M+p are not explained clearly enough to reconstruct the representation.

Generality: The main evidence comes from three closely related simulated manipulation tasks distilled from one multi-task expert, with one task modified to be easier. The MNIST extension uses a nonstandard PCA reduction from 784 to 32 inputs and reports only one aggregate accuracy with no baselines, standard full-input comparison, or uncertainty; it therefore provides weak evidence of transfer beyond the GHN-generated robotics setting.

Limitations/ethics: The limitations section understates rather than analyzes the restricted scope, explicitly asserting that the four-layer limit is “not a limitation.” It does not discuss dependence on GHN-generated and heavily filtered data, fixed maximum width, rollout-based selection, or the possibility that generated embodied policies may behave unpredictably outside simulation. The generic impact statement claims no consequences need highlighting. These are not necessarily prohibitive ethical issues, but they are inadequate treatment of deployment risk and computational cost.

strengths: The paper presents a promising and fairly original combination of GHN-generated weight populations, spatial patch tokenization, and multimodal diffusion for joint architecture and parameter generation. Treating weight matrices as locally structured fields is an interesting direction for weight-space learning.

The generated networks are evaluated by actual execution rather than parameter-space proxies. On three ManiSkill3 tasks, NNiT substantially outperforms D2NWG on held-out architecture configurations; the full-distribution results in Table 9 help show that this is not solely a top-10 selection artifact.

The permutation ablation is valuable: independently permuting neurons preserves network functions and marginal weight statistics but reduces PickCube success from 78.8% to 0%, supporting the conclusion that consistent parameter ordering is important to the method.

The paper includes useful supplementary analyses: comparisons with SGD-generated populations, CKA and parameter-diversity measurements, results for all 80 generated policies, fixed-architecture diversity, joint-sampling architecture diversity, and an MNIST transfer experiment.

Presentation is generally clear and well organized. The distinction between conditional parameter synthesis and joint architecture-weight generation is easy to follow, and the limitations regarding the tested architecture family and scale are acknowledged.

The work could be significant as an initial demonstration of functional policy-weight generation across held-out MLP configurations, especially because robotics control is sensitive to parameter errors.
weaknesses: The central “width-agnostic” and “unseen width” claims are not established. Training and testing both use widths from the same small vocabulary {16,32,64}; only combinations of already-seen widths are held out. Moreover, every parameter block is padded to a fixed maximal H×W grid, so the implementation remains tied to a predefined maximum width. There is no evaluation on a genuinely unseen width such as 24, 48, or a width beyond the training maximum. The demonstrated result is zero-shot topology-combination generalization, which is useful but materially narrower than the title and main claims.

The structural-alignment evidence is suggestive rather than definitive. Repeated magnitude bands and cross-seed correlations demonstrate spatial regularity, but do not by themselves establish neuron-wise semantic alignment or resolution of permutation symmetry. The permutation experiment shows dependence on consistent ordering, not specifically that a CNN-decoded GHN produces the claimed alignment. Comparisons against a non-convolutional GHN decoder, an explicitly canonicalized population, and patch models trained on those controls would make the causal claim substantially stronger.

Baseline fairness and reproducibility are insufficiently documented. Both baselines are adapted to a setting they were not designed for, yet the manuscript gives little detail about those adaptations, architectures, tuning, or training hyperparameters. SANE's near-total failure even on seen architectures raises concern that its implementation is not a meaningful competitive reference. The text also describes D2NWG as using “explicit architecture conditioning” and shortly afterward as “lacking explicit architectural awareness,” which needs clarification.

The main Table 2 numbers select the top 10 of 100 generated policies through an offline validation phase, requiring substantial environment interaction and giving a much more favorable impression than average-sample quality. Table 9 partly remedies this, but average NNiT success is only 78.8%, 74.7%, and 54.9% on the three tasks, rather than the prominently claimed >85%. The exact validation budget and whether selection and final reporting use independent episodes should be specified.

Uncertainty is not evaluated at the level of independent NNiT training runs, dataset-generation runs, or held-out architecture splits. Results appear to come from one fixed split of only eight held-out configurations and one trained generator per task; reported deviations therefore do not establish training robustness or generalization across splits.

Important implementation details are missing, including the NNiT depth and width, attention configuration, patch size, maximum grid size, parameter count, architecture-token decoding procedure, and training compute. The treatment of discrete architecture tokens through continuous Gaussian diffusion and their conversion back to valid categorical widths is especially underspecified. Consequently, the current manuscript is not adequately reproducible despite providing optimizer-level hyperparameters.

The scope is narrow: fixed-depth, fully connected MLPs with a three-value hidden-width vocabulary, task-specific generators, GHN-produced training weights, and a customized easier version of StackCube. The claim that the approach naturally extends to depth or very large networks is speculative, since neither variable-depth generation nor scaling outside the fixed padded grid is tested.

The impact statement is perfunctory, asserting that no consequences need highlighting. Although no immediate severe ethical issue is evident, a more appropriate discussion would acknowledge dual-use and reliability risks from directly generated control policies, as well as the need for validation before real-world robotic deployment.
